topics.title: Pakistan River Systems and Points of Origin
topics.summary: Pakistan's hydro-network is anchored by the Indus River and its eastern and western tributaries, vital for national agriculture, drinking water, and hydro-power generation.
key_facts: Indus River (Sindhu): Originates near Lake Mansarovar in Tibetan Plateau, enters Pakistan through Gilgit-Baltistan, flows approx 3,180 km into Arabian Sea.
Jhelum River: Originates from Verinag Spring in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, joins Chenab at Trimmu.
Chenab River: Originates from Baralacha Pass in Himachal Pradesh (Chandra and Bhaga streams), joins Indus at Panjnad.
Ravi River: Originates near Rohtang Pass in Himachal Pradesh (Bara Bhangal).
Sutlej River: Originates from Lake Rakshastal near Mount Kailash in Tibet.
Panjnad: The confluence where Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej unite before discharging into the Indus at Mithankot.

topics.title: The Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) of 1960 and Strategic Water Security
topics.summary: The landmark water distribution treaty between Pakistan and India brokered by the World Bank, under heightened strategic scrutiny due to upstream hydro-project disputes and climate stress.
key_facts: Signed on September 19, 1960, in Karachi by Field Marshal Ayub Khan and Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru with World Bank mediation.

Water Allocation: Eastern Rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) allocated exclusively to India; Western Rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) allocated to Pakistan, with limited upstream non-consumptive and run-of-the-river power rights granted to India under strict design constraints.
Dispute Resolution Mechanism: 3-tier system: Permanent Indus Commission (PIC), Neutral Expert, and Court of Arbitration at The Hague.
Key Disputes: Kishanganga Hydroelectric Project on Neelum/Jhelum and Ratle Hydroelectric Plant on Chenab River.
Current Challenge: Indian notices seeking unilateral modifications or renegotiation, which Pakistan firmly contests under the treaty's binding international provisions.
Strategic Water Storage: Pakistan's storage capacity is critically low at approximately 30-35 days of average demand compared to the international benchmark of 120-150 days.
potential_interview_questions: Why is the Indus Water Treaty of 1960 of existential strategic significance for Pakistan?
Which rivers were allocated to Pakistan and India respectively under the 1960 Treaty?
Why are storage dams like Diamer-Bhasha and Mohmand critical for national water and energy security?

topics.title: Major Dams, Storage Infrastructure, and Glacial Melting
topics.summary: National dam construction initiatives and climate vulnerabilities stemming from Himalayan-Karakoram-Hindukush glacier retreat.
key_facts: Tarbela Dam: World's largest earth-filled dam on the Indus River in Haripur, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, commissioned in 1976.
Mangla Dam: On Jhelum River in Mirpur, AJK, commissioned in 1967 and raised in 2009 for enhanced storage.
Diamer-Bhasha Dam: Under construction on the Indus River (Gilgit-Baltistan/KPK border); planned live storage of 6.4 MAF and 4,500 MW hydro-power.
Mohmand Dam: Under construction on Swat River; flood mitigation for Peshawar/Charsadda and 800 MW hydro capacity.
Glacial Vulnerability: Pakistan has over 7,200 glaciers—the most outside polar regions; climate change causes Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOF) and long-term water depletion.
potential_interview_questions: How will Diamer-Bhasha and Mohmand dams impact Pakistan's water storage capacity?
What is the threat of climate change and glacial retreat to Pakistan's future water security?
